opponent: attention model (move+position one-hot input, Q/K/V self-attention, WINDOW=6)
condition: blind: the 'AI expected you to play ...' line and its probabilities were hidden during play; they were filled in here from the saved state after the match
strategy_summary: Rounds 1-7: the AI plays randomly, so I used the same all-paper opening as the match with hints. Luck went against me here (1 win, 4 losses, 2 ties).

With the probabilities hidden I still knew two things: the rules from the code (random for 7 rounds, a 6-move window, it plays the counter to its top guess), and therefore its top guess each round, because its move reveals it. What I lost was its confidence.

My method was to work out which follow-ups to my last one to three moves it had seen me play, assume it expects one of those, and play the move that beats or ties the counters to its two likeliest guesses. I also watched for it holding the same guess for several rounds.

Where the missing percentages hurt: I could not tell when it was about to switch guess (round 19), or whether an older memory, a recent memory or its current bias would win (rounds 21, 32, 50). It also learned two real habits of mine, paper after rock and paper after scissors, plus my alternations, which cost rounds 41, 42, 51, 52 and 55.

Result: 27 wins, 18 losses, 25 ties. In the 63 model rounds alone it was 26-14-23. The AI's top guess matched my move in 14 of 63 model rounds (22%). When it was at least 90% confident (20 rounds) it was right 4 times.

Comparison: with hints the same player scored 30-12-28 (27-10-26 in model rounds) and the AI's guess matched in 10 of 63 rounds. One match each way is a small sample, so the gap is suggestive, not proof.
